title: Relations & types of functions
examples: What is the difference between a one-one and an onto function?
How do I check if a relation is transitive?
Can a relation be both symmetric and one-one?

explain.say: Today we look at relations and functions. We check if a relation has special properties. These properties are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. These help us classify relations properly.
A relation is reflexive if every element relates to itself. For example, the relation of 'equals' is always reflexive. Every number equals itself, so it works.
A relation is symmetric if whenever one element relates to another, the reverse is also true. If A relates to B, then B must relate to A. Consider the relation 'is married to'.
A relation is transitive if the link goes all the way through. If A relates to B, and B relates to C, then A must relate to C. Think about 'is less than or equal to'.

draw.text: Transitive: (a, b) and (b, c) implies (a, c)

explain.say: Next we look at functions. A function is one-one if different inputs give different outputs. No two inputs can map to the same output. For example, the function f(x) equals x squared is one-one for positive numbers.

faq.q: What does it mean for a relation to be an equivalence relation?
faq.a: A relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. If it meets all three conditions, it is an equivalence relation. You might also hear it called an equivalence relation.
asks: Is it reflexive, symmetric, and transitive?
What makes a relation an equivalence relation?

faq.q: If a relation is symmetric, does it have to be reflexive?
faq.a: No, a relation can be symmetric without being reflexive. For instance, the relation 'is the parent of' is symmetric if we ignore direction, but it is not reflexive because you are not your own parent. You might also ask if symmetry implies reflexivity.
asks: Must it be reflexive if it is symmetric?
Can a relation be symmetric but not reflexive?

faq.q: How do I test if a function is onto?
faq.a: A function is onto if every element in the target set has a corresponding input. This means the range of the function equals its entire codomain. Another way to say this is that the function covers all possible outputs.
asks: What does it mean for a function to be onto?
Does the range equal the codomain for an onto function?

faq.q: Is being one-one the same as being onto?
faq.a: No, they are different properties. One-one means no two inputs share an output. Onto means every possible output is actually reached by some input. You could ask if they are interchangeable.
asks: One-one versus onto, what is the difference?
Are one-one and onto the same thing?

faq.q: If a relation is reflexive and symmetric, what does that tell me?
faq.a: It tells you that the relation is balanced and every element relates to itself. This is a good start, but you still need to check for transitivity to make it an equivalence relation. You might ask what these two properties imply.
asks: What if it is reflexive and symmetric?
Do I need transitivity if it is reflexive and symmetric?

facts: A relation R on a set A is reflexive if for all a in A, (a, a) is in R.
A relation R is symmetric if for all a and b in A, if (a, b) is in R, then (b, a) is in R.
A relation R is transitive if for all a, b, and c in A, if (a, b) and (b, c) are in R, then (a, c) is in R.
A function f is one-one if f(a) = f(b) implies a = b.

quiz.say: Consider the relation on the set of real numbers defined by x minus y equals zero. Is it reflexive?
quiz.why: The relation requires x minus x to equal zero, which is true for all real numbers.

wrong.0: The definition must hold for all real numbers, not just positive ones.
wrong.1: The definition must hold regardless of the value of y.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might think it only works for zero, but it works for all numbers.

quiz.say: If a function f(x) equals x squared, is it one-one on the set of all real numbers?

options.show: only if the domain is positive
options.say: only if the domain is positive

quiz.why: Because both two and negative two map to four, the function is not one-one.

wrong.0: The one-one property depends only on the inputs mapping uniquely, not the target set size.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake because it works for positive numbers, but the negative inputs break it.
wrong.3: While true, the question asks about the set of all real numbers.

quiz.say: For the relation 'is parallel to' on lines in a plane, if line A is parallel to line B, and line B is parallel to line C, what must be true?

options.show: only if A and C are the same line
options.say: only if A and C are the same line

options.show: line A is parallel to line C
options.say: line A is parallel to line C

quiz.why: This shows the transitive property, which is required for the relation to be transitive.

wrong.0: Parallel lines do not need to be the same line to maintain the relationship.
wrong.1: While it is symmetric, the question specifically tests for transitivity.
wrong.3: This ignores the established geometric rule that parallel lines maintain the relationship.
